cases.abstract: FlexGen targets batched large language model inference when weights and key-value caches exceed GPU memory. Block scheduling reuses loaded weights across GPU batches, while cache offloading permits larger batches; a cost model and linear programming select tensor placement across GPU, CPU, and disk. Without CPU computation, idealized asymptotic weight I/O stays within twice the optimum. In dummy-weight benchmarks with 512-token prompts and 32 generated tokens, OPT-175B on one 16-GB T4, 208-GB CPU memory, and a 1.5-TB SSD reaches 0.69 tokens/s versus 0.01 for uncompressed Accelerate and DeepSpeed. These gains accompany larger effective batches that amortize loaded weights across more prompts. Four-bit weight and cache compression without retraining or calibration raises throughput to 1.12 tokens/s by fitting tensors in CPU memory and avoiding disk swapping. Separate real-weight tests show small Lambada accuracy and WikiText perplexity changes, including sparse value-cache access, but compression can slow models fitting GPU memory. With four GPUs, offloaded models show super-linear decoding scaling but sublinear overall scaling when generating 32 tokens. Seven HELM sub-scenarios with OPT-IML-30B finish in 21 hours including overhead, establishing batch utility under long completion times and substantial host-memory and storage requirements.
cases.notes: Revision connects cache capacity, batch size, and amortized weight transfers (Sections 3-4.3). Tables 2/15 test the throughput consequence; Table 5 separately tests approximation quality with real weights, not a quality-controlled speed experiment. Compression remains a co-contribution because CPU fit removes disk swapping. Appendix A.2 bounds idealized asymptotic weight I/O only. Retained mixed findings: compression overhead and decoding versus overall scaling. HELM establishes completed batch use, not interactive latency. Petals comparisons remain omitted because GPU-count normalization changes comparison scope.

cases.abstract: Neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) models replace discrete hidden-state updates with learned continuous dynamics evaluated by a numerical solver. Adjoint sensitivities compute gradients through a reverse-time augmented ODE without retaining intermediate solver operations, making memory independent of function-evaluation count while tolerances control the precision-computation trade-off. On MNIST, 0.42% error with 0.22 million parameters versus a residual network's 0.41% with 0.60 million supports parameter-efficient classification, not improved accuracy. For dynamics uniformly Lipschitz in state and continuous in time, an instantaneous change-of-variables theorem replaces the Jacobian determinant with a trace in log-density evolution. Trace additivity permits continuous normalizing flows whose density-update cost is linear in hidden-unit count per function evaluation; two-dimensional experiments illustrate density matching and reversible sampling. A latent ODE generates states at irregular observation times from an initial state and shared continuous dynamics, and can incorporate a Poisson likelihood for observation times. On synthetic noisy spirals using 30 of 100 observations, predictive RMSE is 0.1642 versus 0.3937 for an RNN over 100 prediction times extending beyond training observations, supporting reconstruction and extrapolation in this setting. Reverse-time trajectory reconstruction can introduce numerical error; checkpointing can mitigate it by storing intermediate states.
cases.notes: Revision connects continuous dynamics to adjoint training without storing solver steps (Section 2), trace-based density evolution under Theorem 1's conditions (Section 4), and irregular-time prediction from shared latent dynamics (Section 5). Table 1 supports fewer parameters at similar error, not classification superiority; trace additivity explains linear hidden-unit cost. Table 2 tests reconstruction and extrapolation from sampled observations on synthetic spirals. Flow examples remain illustrative because optimizers and iteration budgets differ. Checkpointing retains the numerical-error/memory trade-off; corrupted software names and tolerances remain omitted.
